audit_rationale: Standing governance/availability context was silently converted into immediate dispatch authority; later user correction exposes the mismatch.
The request explicitly referred to both windows; omitting one reply is better explained as attention/completeness failure than intent inference.
The task sequence and dependency boundary admitted multiple readings; the assistant silently chose a mixed sequence and the user immediately reported confusion.
The original request delegated selection of additional questions; the later five-question constraint may be a new preference rather than evidence the earlier broad interpretation was wrong.
The assistant silently privileged stale V1 scope over the newer Saudi brief; the user corrected market, payment and completion scope immediately.
Treating nonexistent production columns as present is a factual/schema error, not an ambiguity about the user’s intent.
The failure is an unreconciled logical contradiction between rules, not silent resolution of user intent.
The issue is incorrect SQL mechanism/syntax; user intent was not materially ambiguous.
The failure arose from a false premise about the chat transport preserving bytes, not from choosing among meanings of the user’s instruction.
The blank-line-only explanation was an unsupported technical inference from byte counts rather than a user-intent branch.
Generalizing a catalog-session observation to PostgREST/service-role behavior is a technical validity error.
The blocking/non-blocking conflict is an engineering consistency defect, not an intent ambiguity.
Confusing a record structure with an operational alert capability is a conceptual/technical overclaim.
The term “additive” was not previously defined; the assistant silently adopted a broad definition and the user supplied a narrower binding meaning.
The two-option framing omitted technically available alternatives; this is primarily solution-space/modeling competence.
The semantic dispute over “byte-identical” is a plausible definition-type intent event, but the stored C0 suggestion “DEFINITION→INTENT” violates the workbook’s own controlled C0 vocabulary.
The first audit turn lacked a retrievable attachment; the failure is an input-availability premise rather than intent inference.
The 35/31 discrepancy came from an erroneous counting method and was corrected by reproducible tooling.
The user explicitly required clearance only for the exact current head and warned later pushes void it; failure to re-check is procedural competence, not ambiguity.
No transcript-observable mismatch is recorded and the strict threshold is consistent with the user’s explicit wording; preserve as a negative/control case, not a positive incident.
Repeat of the missing/wrong attachment premise; useful recurrence evidence but not SII-positive evidence.
The ambiguity was explicitly disclosed and both readings were reported; no silent resolution or mismatch occurred.
This is a meta-extraction decision about where to obtain the transcript, with no mismatch; retain for method audit, not SII analysis.
Retaining a formatting header during a role-framing change is meta-level and no mismatch/consequence is observed.
The authorization language can support more than one reading of whether a genuine GET path should be attempted; no user correction is recorded, so source/context is needed before treating it as SII.
The assistant silently defined “user-defined function” to exclude platform auth helpers, then self-disclosed the sequence deviation; this is a plausible definition/authority IPP.
This is deliberately an inverse/counter-pattern with surfaced ambiguity and no rework. The stored resolution style “ASKED/DISCLOSED” is outside the workbook codebook.
Fresh-clone behavior followed an environment premise and was self-detected; no user-intent mismatch is observed.
“Proof” admits multiple implementation forms, but the user may have delegated method choice. Source context is needed to distinguish legitimate discretion from SII.
The assistant chose rail-only scope without asking; no mismatch is observed and the implementation may have been within delegated discretion.
“NOT MERGED” does not itself resolve whether a remote push is authorized. The push was a silent authority interpretation, but no correction is recorded.
Applying the extraction protocol to the current thread is a meta-method decision and no mismatch is observed.
The instruction explicitly required rebase before every push; stale-base handoff is a compliance/execution failure rather than ambiguity.
Keeping an intentionally red suite out of default CI is a silent scope choice, but no correction occurred and it may be valid delegated test design.
The assistant treated an ordinary two-message case as exhausting the whole C-04 class; the later correction explicitly narrowed what the test could prove.
Choosing a dedicated proof filename is a silent output-form choice, but it appears delegated and was accepted; source is needed before counting it.
The phrase “mirrors the real tenant exactly” may or may not imply mechanical provenance/hash. The later hash requirement could be clarification or a new requirement.
“Marked as reproducing the defect” was silently implemented at suite/name level; the user later required an adjacent greppable label for every assertion.
The commit-time proxy was explicitly disclosed before proceeding and was not corrected; this is useful contrast evidence, not silent inference.
Running TypeScript and build concurrently caused a transient tool collision and was self-corrected; this is execution competence.
As with W38-001, the rebase rule was explicit; stale-base handling is a procedural failure, not intent inference.
The row itself says the original user wording is not observable, violating the extraction protocol’s verbatim-evidence requirement. It cannot enter analysis until the source is recovered.
“Correct only those / add nothing” and “verify every argument” create a genuine scope branch; the assistant silently chose the narrow change-only reading and later broader defects were surfaced.
“Complete corrected file” left transfer channel implicit; the assistant chose a local-link delivery that failed. Both output-intent inference and transport premise contributed.
A bare request label plus attachment left the authorized action underspecified; the assistant chose read-only comparison. Source context is needed to assess intended authority.
“Nothing else” can apply to the entire interaction or only final handback; the assistant silently chose the latter and no correction occurred.
Supplying SQL without an imperative was silently treated as authorization to execute against production. This is a strong authority-type IPP even though the operation was read-only.
The failure arose because Homebrew needed an unwritable log directory; intent to install gh was clear.
The assistant assumed the user could see a device code in tool output; this is an interface/environment premise rather than a meaning choice.
Failure to anticipate parent-directory authorization is an environment/permission premise.
The user specified the outcome (commit + draft PR); the assistant silently elevated one implementation means (local gh authentication) into a prerequisite, causing a multi-turn stall.
The rebase-before-push rule was explicit; failure to keep the branch current is procedural competence rather than ambiguity.
